c.v: Each answer is one rule from the table in the next section. You pass with all six right and a reason for each. Five right is a partial pass. A "valid" for 1 or 5, or an "invalid" for
in 4, shows a rule that needs another look.
An iterator is an object that names a position in a container and knows how to move to the next one. A reference or a pointer names an element's address directly. A view, a

, is a pointer and a length into elements someone else owns. All three are handles, and none owns what it refers to. Invalidation is the point where the standard withdraws its promise about a handle, after some operation on the container. Using it afterward is undefined behaviour, whatever value is still there.

The problem is that a handle can look fine and still be wrong. A container that grows or shrinks may move elements to a new block, breaking a reference into the old one, or leave every element where it was and still break an iterator, because an iterator can promise more than an address, such as which element comes next. Neither failure is a compile error, and a dead handle often still reads a plausible number, so the bug waits for whichever call finally reallocates or rehashes.
The rule is that a reference or a pointer survives exactly as long as its element stays at the same address.
and the hash containers give every element its own heap node and only relink nodes, so inserting, erasing elsewhere, or rehashing never moves one, and references into them survive all of that. A

can move elements: a vector or string that outgrows its block copies everything into a new one, and a deque that grows replaces only its table of block pointers, so a reference into a deque survives a push at either end while every iterator, holding a pointer into that table, does not. A view follows the same rule as an iterator into the same elements.

What this costs you is that nothing checks it at run time, so a stale handle is a bug a passing test can hide. AddressSanitizer catches a handle that reads freed memory, and libstdc++'s debug mode catches an iterator the standard has withdrawn even when its memory hasn't moved, which is why both are worth building with.
You meet this holding a reference to a route's last waypoint across a

That is most of what you need to predict invalidation, because a reference or a pointer to an element is only the element's address: it stays valid exactly as long as the element stays where it is. An iterator can promise more than an address, so it can die while every element stays put. A deque iterator holds four pointers, one of them into the deque's table of blocks, which a push at either end may replace. An unordered container's iterator promises to visit the elements after it, and a rehash reorders the elements, so the standard invalidates the iterators and not the references. A
is a pointer and a length into the owner's elements, so it lives exactly as long as an iterator into the same elements would.

Two shortcuts cover most of the table. The first: an operation that may allocate may invalidate. A vector or a string that grows moves everything, a deque that grows replaces its table of blocks, and an unordered container that grows replaces its buckets.

beforehand, when you know the final size, turns the first case into the second row of the table. The second: erasing an element always invalidates handles to that element, and in a vector or a string it also invalidates everything behind it, because the elements behind shift to close the gap. A deque is stricter still. An erase that takes out neither the first element nor the last invalidates every iterator and every reference into the deque, because it closes the gap by moving whichever side is shorter, which may be the elements in front of the hole.

The string row is the strictest in the table, and deliberately so. The standard doesn't say which calls reallocate, and a string of up to 15 characters keeps them inside the object, where even a move can change them, as the next section shows. So treat every non-const call on a string as the end of every view into it.

Nothing in C++ checks any of this at run time. A dead iterator often still points at memory that holds the right value, so a test passes, and the bug waits for the next reallocation. The worked example shows the two tools that catch it.
